objectives.statement: Distinguish structural and functional divisions of the nervous system and correctly use CNS/PNS anatomical terminology.
Relate the soma, dendrites, axon hillock, axon and terminals to neuronal signalling and maintenance.
Classify neurons structurally and functionally from their processes, locations and direction of information flow.
Explain the organization and directional sequence of chemical synaptic transmission and recognize common synaptic relationships.
Distinguish the six major neuroglial cell types by location and principal function while avoiding outdated abundance and lineage claims.
Compare CNS and PNS myelination and explain how myelin and nodes of Ranvier support rapid conduction.
Distinguish gray matter from white matter using their dominant cellular and axonal components.
Relate endoneurium, perineurium, epineurium and fascicles to peripheral nerve organization and injury localization.
Analyze Wallerian degeneration and the conditions that favour or limit axonal regeneration in the PNS compared with the CNS.
Explain epithelial cellularity, polarity, avascularity, basement-membrane support and regenerative capacity.
Classify epithelia by number of layers and apical cell shape, including pseudostratified and transitional epithelia.
Relate simple squamous, cuboidal and columnar epithelia to their characteristic locations and transport or secretory functions.
Relate stratified squamous, cuboidal, columnar and transitional epithelia to protection and distension.
Explain how apical specializations and gland organization support absorption, transport and secretion.
Explain how cells, fibres and ground substance form the extracellular matrix and determine connective-tissue properties.
Relate collagen, reticular and elastic fibres to tensile strength, supporting networks and recoil.
Distinguish resident and transient connective-tissue cells by origin and principal role.
Classify loose and dense connective tissues and infer tissue identity from fibre arrangement, cells, ground substance and mechanical demand.

questions.stem: A student labels a dark basophilic clump within the middle of an axon as a Nissl body. What is the best correction?
questions.explanation: Classical Nissl substance is found in the soma and proximal dendrites and is absent from the axon and axon hillock. The absolute statement that axons perform no local protein synthesis is too strong, but a Nissl body should not be labelled in the axon.

questions.explanation: A strong response compares Schwann-cell support, endoneurial pathways, debris clearance and target reconnection in the PNS with inhibitory molecules, glial scarring, poor long-distance guidance and different myelin biology in the CNS. It must also state that PNS recovery depends on injury severity, alignment, distance and target viability.

sources.title: OPT 376 Nervous Tissue lecture deck (2024)
Peripheral Nerve Injury

questions.author: Optometry Study Hub authoring team
rubric: Identifies Schwann cells and preserved endoneurial pathways as important PNS guidance structures.
Explains Wallerian degeneration and debris clearance rather than implying the distal axon remains intact.
Contrasts PNS support with inhibitory CNS myelin signals and reactive glial scarring or limited long-distance guidance.
States at least one condition that can still prevent PNS recovery, such as soma death, a large gap, misalignment, scar, long distance or target loss.
Uses cautious language and does not claim that all PNS injuries regenerate or that the CNS has literally zero plasticity or repair.
questions.sampleAnswer: Peripheral regeneration is more favourable when the soma survives and Schwann cells remain aligned within intact endoneurial tubes. The distal segment undergoes Wallerian degeneration, debris is cleared, and proximal sprouts can be guided toward the target. In the CNS, oligodendrocyte-associated inhibitors, reactive glial scarring and the absence of comparable long-distance Schwann-cell tubes limit regrowth. Even in the PNS, a large gap, poor alignment, extensive fibrosis or loss of the target can prevent useful recovery.

questions.author: Optometry Study Hub authoring team
rubric: Chooses a predominantly dense regular architecture with fibres aligned to the main load.
Identifies collagen as the principal tensile element and explains why parallel orientation matters.
Includes a plausible limited elastic-fibre contribution for recoil without making elastic fibres the main tensile component.
Identifies fibroblasts/fibrocytes as the dominant resident matrix-maintaining cells and notes relatively little ground substance.
Describes vascularity cautiously as limited or relatively sparse rather than claiming all connective tissue is highly vascular or completely avascular.
questions.sampleAnswer: The ligament should be predominantly dense regular connective tissue, with type I collagen bundles aligned parallel to the main tensile axis. A smaller population of elastic fibres could permit modest recoil. Fibroblasts should lie between the bundles and maintain the matrix, with relatively little ground substance. Vascularity would be limited compared with loose connective tissue, so repair would be slower. A random dense irregular pattern would waste tensile strength in the principal loading direction.
